profile.name: Brejesh Balakrishnan
profile.headline: AI Engineer · Agentic AI and Evaluation
summaryBullets: AI Engineer at Cloud202 (UK, remote). I work on governance and safety controls for AI agents built on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore.
On my own time I build agent and RAG systems and then test them the hard way: baselines, pass marks written down first, confidence intervals, and write-ups that include what missed.
Before this I spent almost two years shipping Java and Spring Boot on AWS at Accenture, which is where my habits around tests, profiling and code review come from.

projects.title: Agent GovBench
projects.oneLine: An open benchmark that measures whether guardrails actually stop a tool-using AI agent from being misused.
projects.description: Guardrails for agents get sold on claims, so I built a way to measure them. Agent GovBench runs a Google ADK agent with 9 tools across 5 stub MCP servers on Google Cloud, against 999 synthetic scenarios. 45% of them are ordinary requests that only look risky, so a guard can't win by blocking everything. Attack success is scored from the tool-call log by a deterministic check, not by an LLM judge alone.
highlights: Model Armor at its MEDIUM injection threshold blocked 29.8% of malicious calls and flagged 27.1% of benign ones. A Gemini Flash guard blocked 94.7% and flagged 0.4%, measured with the agent in the loop.
Attack success comes from the tool-call log with a deterministic check, so the result doesn't depend on an LLM judge's quirks.
The benign twins are deliberate: 45% of scenarios are legitimate requests that look risky, which is what exposes over-blocking.
Published the harness and sanitized data with bootstrap intervals and written limits. Agent Gateway governance is logged as not tested, not estimated.

projects.title: Toolcall Guard
projects.oneLine: A small free guard model that checks one agent tool call before it runs, plus a cascade that only pays for Gemini when the local model is unsure.
projects.description: I distilled a hosted Gemini guard into Gemma 4 E4B with LoRA, so a laptop can look at a proposed tool call and answer allow or block with a category and a one-line reason. Then I judged it on 1,566 real agent calls from Agent GovBench instead of only its own synthetic test set. It blocks 62% of attacks at 8% false positives, which is not good enough to be a sole gate. So I added a cascade, an MCP server and a static site where you can try it with your own key.
highlights: Tuning cut false positives from 15% to 8% at about the same recall. It did not make the free model a safe sole gate, and the write-up says so.
4-bit quantization dropped real-traffic recall to 35%, which is why the laptop version is a screen and not a gate.
The cascade sends 69% of calls to Gemini and still blocks 98% with 2% false positives on 981 held-out calls, at USD 2.43 per 1,000 calls against 3.42 for Flash alone (about 29% cheaper).
Compared on Agent GovBench traffic because my synthetic test set was labelled by Pro (circular) and written by Flash (advantaged).
Family-hash splits with leakage checks. Total recorded spend: USD 67.50.

projects.title: Compliance Workbench
projects.oneLine: Ask which EU and US rules apply to your AI, data or cyber product. Answers quote the official text, show the start date, and decline what they don't cover.
projects.description: A RAG assistant over 3,946 provisions from 9 official texts, including the EU AI Act, GDPR, NIS2, DORA, the Cyber Resilience Act and NIST. It started as an 8-node LangGraph backend and grew into three tools: Ask, a checklist of 112 duty-bearing articles, and a gap check that compares a pasted policy with the law. Declining is a feature here, and I measured it. It is information from official text, not legal advice.
highlights: Right article in the top 6 on 50 hand-labelled questions: recall 0.847, MRR 0.862. I set the labels by reading the documents, not by running my own retriever.
Declined 13 of 14 questions about rules it doesn't cover, with no model call, and wrongly declined 0 of 50 covered ones.
The gap check never called a planted gap covered in any run. Each verdict quotes both the law and the policy, checked word for word.
Every start date carries a verbatim quote of the law, and a test fails the build if a date or quote isn't in the source data.
Earlier, I A/B tested a hosted reranker, found it net negative (nDCG@3 down 0.057, latency up 435 ms) and switched it off.
Ten prompt-injection cases with no breaches, 677 offline tests, and the same tools are available over MCP.

projects.title: Otaku Oracle
projects.oneLine: An anime Q&A site where the model drafts an answer and a deterministic checker marks every claim against AniList as verified, conflict or unchecked.
projects.description: I wanted to see whether AI answers could be made easier to check. The model writes a draft, then a checker compares each claim with the AniList record and shows agreement, conflict or unchecked. I pre-registered the evaluation before running it: 18 titles, 124 questions, 744 pairs per model, answered with and without the record in context.
highlights: Grounding raised exact-match accuracy by 38.7 points pooled (95% CI 31.7 to 46.0). On glm-4.7-flash it went from 54.6% to 99.2%. It cleared the pass rule I wrote down first.
The caveat is in the write-up: the grounded arm contains the answer, so it measures faithful reading of a record, not whether AniList is right.
AniList returned 403 to Cloudflare Worker IPs, so a small Vercel relay sits in front of it, protected by a shared-secret header.
Every Jikan and Wikidata call was failing silently because Cloudflare Workers reject redirect mode error. Fixed, with a regression test.
Multi-source cross-checking is switched off on the live site because Jikan timed out from Cloudflare. Claims verify against AniList alone.

projects.title: Feasible Day
projects.oneLine: A planner that builds walkable one to three day itineraries from OpenStreetMap and shows which opening-hours and walking-time checks each plan passed.
projects.description: LLM day plans look tidy, but the museum may be closed that Monday or the walk may not fit the gap. I measured it: two open LLMs produced a fully feasible day in 2 of 576 runs. So I built a planner on OpenStreetMap that checks every stop against opening hours and every transfer against walking time, and I wrote the pass criteria before writing any of its code.
highlights: On 96 pre-registered test days in 12 cities, Llama 3.3 70B and Llama 3.1 8B (3 runs per day each) gave 2 feasible days out of 576. The planner passes 96 of 96 on its own rules.
Re-timed with an independent routing engine (OSRM), 94.8% of plans still hold up, just under the 95% threshold I set. I left the miss in.
In 15 cities added later, only 59% of plans pass that routing check. The app shows it instead of tuning it away. My guess is rivers and rail lines, and I haven't tested it.
Caught my own error: an early figure for unreal places in LLM plans was a map-coverage artefact, so I split the metric and stopped claiming a hallucination rate.
Free to run: a static app with no server and no runtime keys. The monthly update job has a hard USD 1.50 LLM cap and measured USD 0.0079 for 18 calls.

projects.title: SafetyOps Copilot
projects.oneLine: Turns a workplace safety observation into an explainable assessment, an action with an owner and a due date, and a shift handover.
projects.description: It began as an event-driven ML pipeline: DistilBERT severity scoring, YOLOv8 hard-hat detection and a LangGraph triage brief. Then I asked what would give a safety coordinator a reason to come back tomorrow, because a prediction alone doesn't give anyone ownership. The new workspace tracks corrective actions, needs evidence to close them, and exports a handover as Markdown, CSV or JSON. A local MCP server shares the assessment logic with agents, read-only.
highlights: DistilBERT fine-tuned on MSHA mine-safety narratives and tested on 1,605 held-out reports: macro-F1 0.78 against 0.34 for a rule baseline, and high-severity recall 0.88 against 0.16.
Every assessment says which path produced it (trained model or a labelled rule fallback) and shows its priority arithmetic. Model loading never blocks a save.
Closing an action needs a note, and revision checks stop a stale tab from overwriting newer work.
The read-only MCP server has three tools and was tested with the official SDK client. It can't read browser records or close an action.
The live check on Cloud Run caught a missing Secure cookie flag behind the proxy. I fixed it and added a regression test before moving traffic.

projects.title: Mozhi
projects.oneLine: A Tamil, Malayalam and English voice assistant where a 2 ms trained router replaces LLM prompting, declines what it can't do, and speaks at the respect level you choose.
projects.description: The first version asked a small LLM to pick a tool from a prompt, and nobody had measured it. When I did, the answer was valid on 55% of requests, took 3.3 seconds, and it acted on 40.7% of requests it should have declined. So I replaced the LLM with a fine-tuned MiniLM router (23 MB, int8 ONNX). It runs as a Windows app and entirely in the browser. Tamil and Malayalam came later, with a five-level respect meter because you is not one word in either language.
highlights: The router scores 0.941 action macro-F1 (95% CI 0.916 to 0.962) on 2,805 test requests with 0.8% false actions and a 2.2 ms median. The best constrained LLM prompt scored 0.879 at 1,047 ms.
Pass marks were pre-registered. I ran 3 seeds with bootstrap intervals against 12 compared systems and reported the thresholds I missed.
Closed a 10-point speech gap by training on 6,600 real Whisper transcripts: 0.929 routing macro-F1 on medium.en.
The Tamil and Malayalam router is a first model that misses its own target: 0.82 and 0.81 against 0.85. The wording still needs a native speaker's review.
The optional LLM sits behind a spend guard: monthly budget, daily call cap, reserve before the call, fail closed.
1,475 public-domain verses and 14 folk-tale summaries in my own words, with the source shown on each.

projects.title: Toonforge
projects.oneLine: A private photo-to-comic-print studio in the browser, with edge-aware smoothing, reusable recipes, an optional text-model planner and a local MCP server.
projects.description: The original repo's API tests passed while real inference couldn't produce a valid PNG, because the tests mocked the bytes. I rebuilt it as deterministic image processing in a Web Worker: edge-aware smoothing, tone quantization and Sobel outlines, with a histogram panel and twelve saved recipes. A text model can propose filter settings and you review them before Apply. The photo never leaves the device. This is classical computer vision, not a trained or generative model.
highlights: The text model sees an instruction, the current settings and three aggregate statistics, never pixels or filenames. Its reply is checked against an allowlist and bounded numbers before you can apply it.

On seeded targets against posterization and box smoothing, flat-region noise drops from about 30 to 0 and boundary contrast stays at 127 against 63 for box smoothing. Thin low-contrast lines get weaker, and that is documented.
A local MCP server (list_styles, analyze_png, plan_edit, render_png) shares the production engine, with canonical path checks, size limits and non-overwriting output.
CI downloads and re-imports a real exported PNG from the live site, which is the check the original project was missing.
Automated accessibility scans at 390, 768 and 1440 px, plus offline reload and print-race tests.

projects.title: Kindred
projects.oneLine: Name one title you loved and get its kin across anime, manga, manhwa, manhua, novels, movies and series, ranked in your browser.
projects.description: Recommenders learn from people who rated the same things, and almost nobody rates an anime and its manga in one place. On an AniList sample there are 49,441 recommendation links inside a single format and zero from an anime to a manga. So Kindred reads what titles are about, learns a small taste adapter from the links that do exist, and ranks 12,809 titles per query in the browser from about 5 MB of static files.
highlights: On a benchmark I pre-registered, Kindred reaches 0.217 NDCG@10 against 0.142 for the best non-learned baseline. The test split was scored once and a rerun reproduces the results byte for byte.
With no cross-medium labels, the benchmark walks the one bridge that exists: fans of anime A also like anime B, and B was adapted from manga T.

Three of my pre-registered hypotheses failed and are published. Sentence embeddings alone lost to curated tags (0.121 against 0.142), and on MovieLens plain item-kNN beat content scoring by 3 to 5 times.
The browser engine is tested against the Python reference on the shipped files, so the numbers on the page describe what actually runs.
Honest limits: proxy labels rather than human judgments, and live action is not validated across media.

projects.title: Analytics Copilot (Text-to-SQL)
projects.oneLine: Mistral-7B fine-tuned with QLoRA to turn plain questions into schema-aware SQL, with an evaluation harness I wrote from scratch.
projects.description: A full fine-tuning pipeline: dataset curation, QLoRA training, a custom two-benchmark evaluation and publishing to the Hub, wrapped in a serving layer shaped like production. Mistral-7B-Instruct is tuned with 4-bit NF4 quantization and LoRA adapters (r=16) on all seven attention and MLP projections. The Streamlit front end carries no GPU or ML dependencies, so training and serving stay separate.
highlights: Under 1% of parameters trained, using 4-bit NF4 quantization and LoRA r=16 adapters across seven projection matrices.
The harness checks exact match, literal-masked match, sqlglot parse validity and AST schema adherence, which catches hallucinated tables and columns that string similarity misses.
In-domain: 35.0% exact match, 100% parse success and 97.5% schema adherence. Zero-shot on Spider the schema adherence is 76%, which puts a number on the generalization gap.
Inference fails over from a Hugging Face Endpoint with adapter routing to OpenAI, and a separate wake-up ping warms the endpoint so warm-ups never trigger the failure path.
A CI break with 271 lint violations turned out to be upstream linter drift. A 9-line config pin fixed it, with no repo-wide reformat.

projects.title: Customer Churn Prediction
projects.oneLine: A leakage-safe churn model with Optuna-tuned XGBoost, SHAP-grounded explanations and a full MLOps loop, deployed live.
projects.description: End-to-end churn prediction on the public IBM Telco sample dataset (7,043 records, 26.5% churn). Six models were benchmarked under 5-fold stratified CV on PR-AUC, XGBoost was tuned with Optuna, and the decision threshold of 0.174 comes from an explicit 5:1 false-negative to false-positive cost. An explanation layer feeds SHAP drivers to an LLM, with retention tactics retrieved through sentence-transformers and FAISS.
highlights: Test PR-AUC 0.66, ROC-AUC 0.85 and recall 0.87, with an optimism gap of 0.01.
A two-tier faithfulness check on the explanations exposed a real grounding bug. Fixing it lifted faithfulness from 0.72 to 0.90 (n=50, seeded).
One Pandera data contract is shared by training and serving, so the test suite fails if the API schema drifts.
Evidently drift monitoring with a retrain rule, an MLflow champion and challenger registry, and a CI gate that blocks merges below a PR-AUC floor.
Cut the Docker image by 57% (11.4 GB to 4.9 GB) with CPU-only torch and a split UI image.

projects.title: Outside
projects.oneLine: An outing planner that checks every hour of a 1 to 8 hour window against your weather preferences and explains the closest alternative when nothing fits.
projects.description: A daily high or a single pleasant hour doesn't answer whether you can get outside for two uninterrupted hours. Outside compares up to two cities over three days, requires every hour of a window to fit, and ranks the windows. When nothing matches it shows the closest fit and lists exactly what you would be giving up. The same planning engine is available through an optional local MCP server.
highlights: The exact-ranking path agrees with an independent exhaustive reference on 3,000 of 3,000 deterministic cases with zero constraint violations. That is evidence about the software, not about forecast accuracy.
The check covers interior hours, not just the first one, because a pleasant start can hide a wet second hour.
Missing values and thunderstorm codes are excluded from both exact matches and alternatives. Nothing gets softened to manufacture a suggestion.
Timezone handling uses the forecast location's clock and real seconds for contiguity. Calendar export uses UTC.

projects.title: Gambit Realms
projects.oneLine: A browser chess game with eight measured opponents, a coach that warns before you lose material, and animated captures in four realms.
projects.description: I rebuilt a 220-line pygame chess app to answer one question: can a browser-only engine give a beginner an opponent that makes beginner mistakes, and a coach that warns before a piece is hung? I wrote five targets down first, then ran 3,560 games. Three were met and two were not, and both misses are on the Evidence page of the live site.
highlights: Eight levels rated 950 to 2600+ on Stockfish's own Elo scale. Each level beats the one below it in 7 of 7 pairs.
Coach recall is 75.4%, but precision is 64.8% against my 85% target. About 1 alarm in 3 is false.
The bug that looked like Stockfish crashing at 300k nodes was my adapter sending commands from inside the engine's own callback. Found by bisecting the command sequence.
Review caught a circular coach label and fabricated-looking intervals in the first evaluation harness. Both were fixed and logged before the reporting run.
Static site of 2.5 MB, with unit, browser and accessibility checks in CI.

projects.title: Inventory Bin Classification
projects.oneLine: ResNet-50 transfer learning on 10,000+ warehouse images, tuned with SageMaker and served from a live endpoint.
projects.description: A computer vision pipeline that classifies how many items are in a warehouse bin. Splits are deterministic and stored as S3 ImageFolder channels. SageMaker Bayesian tuning with 2-instance distributed training on managed spot instances improved macro-F1 by about 22% over the baseline, and the model is served through a real-time endpoint with a custom PyTorch handler and an AWS Lambda in front.
highlights: About 22% macro-F1 gain from Bayesian tuning over learning rate, weight decay, batch size and backbone freezing.
The Lambda takes an image URL or S3 URI and returns a label, confidence and class probabilities as JSON.
Cleaned up every resource afterwards, so no endpoints or storage were left running.

projects.title: Navigation Aid for Visually Impaired Users
projects.oneLine: A wearable that combines an ultrasonic sensor with camera-based object detection and speaks short alerts, built on a Raspberry Pi 4.
projects.description: My final-year project at College of Engineering Guindy, built with a team of four under Dr. T. Sridarshini. The device pairs an HC-SR04 proximity sensor with an object detector and turns detections into spoken alerts, with a 2 second debounce so the user isn't flooded with speech. It was my first real experience of an ML result that had to run on small hardware.
highlights: Added a Convolutional Block Attention Module and replaced IoU with DIoU for box regression. That gave a 3.3% accuracy increase over baseline SSD on COCO: 0.96 accuracy, 0.963 precision and 450 ms inference, with the biggest gain on small objects.
Benchmarked six alternatives from a four-paper literature survey, plus ultrasonic-only sensing.
Ultrasonic alone covers 2 cm to 2 m at 40 degrees. The camera pipeline covers 30 cm to 6 m at 78 to 108 degrees, so the two sensors fill each other's gaps.

bullets: Audited governance and safety in Qubitz, the company's platform for building AI agents on AWS, against the 4 projects in AWS's sample AI agent factory, covering 15+ governance features.
Wrote a phased plan, since approved, for building governance controls into the platform and into the agents it creates on Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore.

Researched Amazon SageMaker for features that could extend the company's enterprise offering across client projects, alongside 7 AWS trainings and accreditations in sales, technical, cloud economics and agentic AI.
Cut slow API responses (over 5 seconds) from roughly 80% of calls to under 20% on a Java and Spring Boot financial services platform on AWS, through profiling, SQL query tuning and caching.
Delivered 200+ story points across Agile sprints, turning loosely written requirements into shipped features alongside UI and QA teammates, and presented sprint demos to client stakeholders.
Kept automated test coverage above 90% across unit, contract and BDD suites, built proper regression suites, and closed critical defects through root-cause analysis.
Onboarded 3 new joiners: local setup, background on the client and team, a walkthrough of their first sprint and code reviews.
Researched natural language to SQL approaches and reviewed commercial products, documenting accuracy against complexity and cost to shape the early product direction.
Validated SQL Server replication and synchronization checks across large tables, then documented the findings and handoffs for the team.
Trained and cross-validated regression and classification models in Python and scikit-learn on structured business data, to build a car recommendation system.
Did the exploratory analysis, cleaning and feature preparation in Pandas, and presented findings to non-technical stakeholders with Seaborn and Matplotlib visuals.
Built and maintained a structured database of potential sponsors, and supported outreach and follow-ups.
Helped plan and run a coding event, which meant working with stakeholders and delivering under deadlines.
Did desk research and drafted sections of an EU Horizon 2020 proposal on Integrated Local Energy Systems and a CIFAR Responsible AI proposal under the Canada Solution Network (STAR RAISE).
Coordinated incubation activities, including startup interactions and site visits for programs on innovation, climate and gender inclusion.
